entries.meaning: Points at more than one thing near the speaker — in the room, in the present stretch of time, or in the part of the discussion currently in hand.
examples: These are the files you asked for.
Are these yours, or did somebody leave them behind?
I'll take these and leave the rest.
These were selling for twice as much last month.
These don't fit anymore.
These are my parents, Ray and Dolores.
Everything in the box is cracked except these.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — the vowel stays long even in fast speech, because the demonstrative carries the stress in its clause
entries.русский: эти — указательное местоимение мн. числа о близком; ставится только с мн. числом глагола
entries.case: none — one form serves as subject, object, and object of a preposition
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: demonstrative pronoun (plural, proximal)
entries.person / number: third person plural; no gender distinction, no case forms
entries.refers to: more than one thing near the speaker — near in the room, in the present stretch of time, or in the part of the conversation currently open. It points at objects freely; it points at people only in the introducing frame These are my parents, never as an ordinary subject for people already known (✗ These are exhausted → They are exhausted). Unlike singular this, it cannot take a single clause as its antecedent — one clause counts as one thing, so this or that handles it — though it can gather up two or more statements at once (They cut the budget and froze hiring. These are the reasons we can't hire.).
entries.agreement: plural verb, always — These are the ones. These were on sale. These don't fit. Never ✗ these is. If what you are pointing at is singular or uncountable, the pronoun changes rather than the verb: This is the last of it.
entries.pattern: these + [plural verb] · [verb] these (I'll take these) · [preposition] these (with these, out of these) · these are [plural noun phrase] (identifying) · these … those (contrastive pair) · these + reduced relative (these left over from Friday)
entries.contrast: Two axes cross. Number — these is the plural of this and takes plural countable referents only. Distance — these is near (in space, in the current stretch of time, or in what is still live in the talk), where those is away, past, or finished. Pronoun against determiner — the pronoun is the whole noun phrase (these are taken, I'll take these), the determiner leans on a noun (these seats are taken). Two smaller traps: the partitive idiom is those of us / those of you whatever the distance, never ✗ these of us; and these ones, ordinary in speech and in Canadian and British usage, is struck out by most American copy editors — write these, or these two, or the red ones.
entries.see also: this, those, that, those of, these ones / those ones, these here, these (determiner)

entries.meaning: Points at a single thing — or a mass, a moment, or an idea — that is near the speaker: near in the room, near in time, or near in the flow of the conversation.
examples: This is the last of the coffee.
Take this and put it in the mail.
They cut the budget again. This is why we can't hire.
Listen to this: they want the whole report by Friday.
Is this yours?
This is my sister, Nadia.
This doesn't feel right to me.
I've had about enough of this.

senses.head: In space
body: The thing near me, or nearer than the alternative: This is the one I meant, not that.

senses.head: In time
body: The stretch of time containing now, when it is the subject of comment: This is the busiest week of the year.

senses.head: Pointing back at a whole clause
body: They cut the budget again. This is why we can't hire. Standard, and the source of the vagueness problem above.

senses.head: Pointing forward
body: Listen to this: / It comes down to this: — the demonstrative announces something the hearer has not heard yet. That cannot do this.

senses.head: Identifying and introducing people
body: Face to face, This is my sister, Nadia; on the telephone, This is Karen or, answering for oneself, This is she — see this is he / this is she.
examples: This is the last of the coffee.
Take this and put it in the mail.
They cut the budget again. This is why we can't hire.
Listen to this: they want the whole report by Friday.
Is this yours?
This is my sister, Nadia.
This doesn't feel right to me.
I've had about enough of this.

entries.pronunciation note: keeps its full vowel as a pronoun; the casual /ðəs/ heard in this morning belongs to the unstressed determiner, and a standalone this is normally the stressed word in its clause
entries.русский: это, этот — указывает на близкое, а также на целую высказанную или предстоящую мысль
entries.case: none — one form for every position
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: demonstrative pronoun (singular, proximal)
entries.person / number: third person singular; no gender distinction, no case forms
entries.refers to: one thing near the speaker, or a mass of something (This is the last of the coffee); a stretch of time containing now; a whole preceding clause or idea (They cut the budget again. This is why we can't hire.); and, pointing forward, something the speaker is about to say or show (Listen to this:). With people it is limited to introducing and identifying — This is my sister, and on the phone This is Karen — never for a person already established (✗ This is exhausted → She is exhausted).
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — This is mine. This was expensive. This doesn't work. The verb agrees with this and with nothing downstream of it: This is the reason our costs went up, This is what the neighbors complained about. With an amount the singular holds even though the complement is plural in form — This is forty dollars' worth, This is three hours of work. But when the referent itself is plural and countable, the pronoun changes rather than the verb: These are my keys, not ✗ This is my keys.
entries.pattern: this + [singular verb] · [verb] this (Read this) · [preposition] this (after this, because of this) · this is [noun phrase] (identifying or introducing) · this pointing forward, followed by a colon and the thing itself (It comes down to this:) · this is + [personal pronoun] on the telephone (This is he) · this … that (contrastive pair)
entries.contrast: Against that. Proximity in space, but in discourse something subtler: this keeps a topic open and that closes it. Pointing back at the same fact, That settles it means the matter is done, while This changes everything means we now have to deal with it. Pointing forward, only this works — ✓ Listen to this:, ✗ Listen to that: about something not yet said. Against these. Number, and the boundary is absolute. Pronoun against determiner. The pronoun stands alone (this is late); the determiner leans on a noun (this report is late). The writing trap. A this whose antecedent is an entire clause is not ungrammatical — it is everywhere in speech and in good journalism — but in formal prose it makes the reader guess, and the standard repair is to attach a summary noun: not This means we're behind, but This delay means we're behind.
entries.see also: these, that, this one / that one, this and that, this is he / this is she, this here, this (determiner)

entries.meaning: Points at a single thing, a mass, a finished time, or a whole idea that is away from the speaker — across the room, back in the past, or already dealt with in the conversation.
examples: That is the best offer you're going to get.
They cancelled the trip a week out. That surprised everyone.
Who's that at the door?
Don't ever say that to your mother again.
After that, nobody brought it up again.
That wasn't what I meant.
Is that all you're taking?
That's my brother in the blue jacket.

senses.head: In space
body: The thing farther off, or nearer the hearer: Hand me that, would you? A gesture or a glance usually goes with it.

senses.head: In time
body: A stretch of time cut off from now: That was the summer we lived in Denver.

senses.head: Pointing back at a whole clause or idea
body: They cancelled the trip a week out. That surprised everyone. The demonstrative treats what was said as finished and comments on it.

senses.head: Identifying
body: Who's that at the door? / That's my brother in the blue jacket. This is the one frame in which a demonstrative pronoun may refer to a person.

senses.head: Substituting for a repeated noun
body: In formal writing, that of replaces a singular or uncountable noun already named: a climate like that of Spain. See that of.
examples: That is the best offer you're going to get.
They cancelled the trip a week out. That surprised everyone.
Who's that at the door?
Don't ever say that to your mother again.
After that, nobody brought it up again.
That wasn't what I meant.
Is that all you're taking?
That's my brother in the blue jacket.

entries.pronunciation note: never reduced — the demonstrative pronoun always keeps the full vowel /ðæt/; the weak /ðət/ belongs to the two other words spelled that, the relative pronoun and the conjunction, and that difference is the fastest way to tell them apart by ear
entries.русский: то, тот — указывает на далёкое или прошедшее, а также на всё только что сказанное
entries.case: none — one form for every position
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: demonstrative pronoun (singular, distal)
entries.person / number: third person singular; no gender distinction, no case forms
entries.refers to: one thing away from the speaker, or a mass, or a finished stretch of time; a whole preceding clause, sentence, or run of discourse (They cancelled the trip. That surprised me.), which is its most characteristic job and one no other pronoun but it does as cleanly; and, in that of, a noun already named. With people it is confined to identifying — Who's that? — That's my brother — and once the person is established English switches to he, she, or they: ✗ That went home early.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — That is enough. That was a mistake. That doesn't help. Plural referents take those. A singular complement, and an amount, both keep the singular: That is the reason the numbers moved, That is twenty dollars. A plural complement is the one soft spot: That was my parents at the door is ordinary speech, but edited prose changes the pronoun along with the verb — Those were my parents.
entries.pattern: that + [singular verb] · [verb] that (Don't say that) · [preposition] that (after that, besides that, with that) · that's [noun phrase] (identifying) · that of [noun phrase] (formal substitution) · that which [clause] (formal) · frozen idioms: at that, that is, that said, that's that
entries.contrast: Three separate contrasts share this headword. Against this: distance and discourse status — that is away, past, finished, or the hearer's; this is near, current, mine, or still to come. Responding to something another person has just said, Americans overwhelmingly reach for that (That's a good point, That's not what I heard). Against those: number. Against the other two thats: the demonstrative pronoun is stressed /ðæt/ and can be replaced by this; the relative (the car that we sold) and the conjunction (I know that she left) reduce to /ðət/ and can usually be dropped. Apply both tests — swap in this, then try deleting — and the demonstrative is the only one that accepts this and the only one that cannot go. The deletion test has a limit: a relative that can be dropped only when it is the object of its own clause, so the car that broke down keeps it. And the same writing caution as this: pointing at a whole clause is standard, but in formal prose give it a summary noun (That decision surprised everyone).
entries.see also: this, those, this one / that one, that of, that which, that's that, that's it, at that, that (relative), that (determiner)

entries.meaning: Points at more than one thing away from the speaker, or picks out a class of people or things that the following clause or phrase then defines.
examples: Those are the files you requested.
I'd rather have those than these.
The results are consistent with those reported last year.
Those who registered early get priority seating.
Those of us who commute know the 8:10 is never on time.
Are those still under warranty?
Those weren't the instructions we were given.
Those were the days.

senses.head: In space and in plural pointing
body: Those are the files you requested. The plural counterpart of pointing that.

senses.head: "The ones" — substituting for a repeated plural noun
body: Followed by a participle or a phrase: results consistent with those reported last year. Formal, and it saves repeating the noun.

senses.head: "Those who" — the people who
body: Names a group by what is true of them: those who registered early. See those who.

senses.head: "Those of us" and "those of you"
body: A partitive that includes the speaker or the hearer: those of us who commute. The idiom takes those no matter how near the group is — never ✗ these of us.

senses.head: Nostalgic and idiomatic
body: Those were the days. Fixed, always plural, always past.
examples: Those are the files you requested.
I'd rather have those than these.
The results are consistent with those reported last year.
Those who registered early get priority seating.
Those of us who commute know the 8:10 is never on time.
Are those still under warranty?
Those weren't the instructions we were given.
Those were the days.

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — full diphthong, and normally the stressed word in its clause
entries.русский: те — указательное местоимение мн. числа о далёком; также в оборотах those who, those of
entries.case: none — one form for every position
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: demonstrative pronoun (plural, distal)
entries.person / number: third person plural; no gender distinction, no case forms
entries.refers to: more than one thing away from the speaker; plural items already mentioned; and, in the frames those who, those that/which, and those of, a class of people or things defined by whatever follows. Like these, it cannot take a single clause as its antecedent — that job belongs to singular this and that — though it can sum up two or more statements at once (The plant closed and the road washed out. Those are the two facts that matter.). It reaches people in two frames: identifying, exactly as these does (Those are my cousins, over by the window), and in front of a relative clause, where those who apply early means the people who apply early. For a person already established it is out: ✗ Those are always late → They are always late.
entries.agreement: plural verb — Those are mine. Those were the days. Those don't match. Inside the those who frame both verbs stay plural: Those who arrive late are seated at intermission. Two traps follow from that. After those of us, the relative clause agrees with us, first person plural: those of us who are on call, not ✗ who is on call. And one of those … who takes a plural verb, because the relative clause describes the plural noun: He's one of those people who never answer email — the singular answers is common in speech and is corrected in edited prose.
entries.pattern: those + [plural verb] · [verb] those · [preposition] those · those who [clause] · those that / those which [clause] · those of [noun phrase] · those of us / you / them who [clause] · those + reduced relative or participle (those left behind, those reported last year, those responsible)
entries.contrast: Against these: distance. Against that: number. Pronoun against determiner — the determiner sits on a noun (those people), the pronoun replaces it (those are the ones). Against a bare comparison — when a plural noun is being compared, the substitution is obligatory in formal writing: ✗ Our returns are higher than our competitors (returns against people) → than those of our competitors, or in plain American English than our competitors'. Against nonstandard them: Those are the ones is standard, Them are the ones is dialect. And those ones, like these ones, is speech-only in American English; edited prose writes those or the ones.
entries.see also: these, that, those who, those of, those which, these ones / those ones, them, those (determiner)

entries.meaning: Picks out more than one countable thing by pointing at it — the plural of this one, ordinary in speech and edited out of American prose.
examples: These ones are cracked; put them in the other box. (speech — edited prose: These are cracked)
Not the big ones — these ones, right here in front. (speech, contrastive)
Do you want these ones or the plain ones?
Those ones were on sale last week, and now they aren't. (speech)
Canadian and British writing takes it without comment: Those ones were sold at the fair.
American edited prose: Those were sold at the fair. / The ones on the left were sold at the fair.
Nonstandard: Them ones ain't ripe yet.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — ones takes the stress and keeps its full vowel, and the /z/ of these runs straight into the /w/, so the phrase is one unit, [ˌðiˈzwʌnz]
entries.русский: эти, те (предметы) — разг.; в американской печати вычёркивают, пишут these / those
entries.register: ordinary in American speech; struck out of American edited prose; unremarkable in Canadian and British usage, spoken and written
entries.type: demonstrative + the prop-word ones — a plural noun phrase with the noun left out
entries.person / number: third person plural
entries.refers to: more than one countable thing already named or in view, picked out by nearness (these ones) or by distance (those ones). The prop-word needs something countable behind it: there is no mass-noun version (✗ these ones of coffee), and no singular ✗ this ones. It points at objects; for people the identifying frame takes bare these and those (Those are my cousins), and those ones about people sounds dismissive.
entries.agreement: plural verb — These ones are cracked. Those ones were on sale. Never ✗ these ones is.
entries.pattern: these ones / those ones as subject or object · [preposition] these ones · the ones + relative clause (the standard substitute — the ones we ordered) · these two, those three (the numeral substitute) · the red ones, the big ones (the adjective substitute)
entries.contrast: Against bare these and those — the ones adds no meaning an American editor will pay for: These are cracked says everything these ones are cracked says, and this is one of the handful of things American copy editors delete on sight. It is worth being clear about what kind of objection that is: it is not a grammatical error and it is not dialect — it is normal in American speech, normal in Canada, normal in Britain, and simply not printed in American edited prose. Against the ones — the ones is standard everywhere and is the form to write when a relative clause follows (the ones that came in Tuesday), which bare those handles less comfortably. Against this one / that one — the singular pair draws no objection at all, in any variety, which is the clearest evidence that the complaint is about the redundant plural and not about the prop-word. A note on what is a determiner here — inside the phrase, these is a determiner sitting on the noun-like ones; it is the whole phrase, not the demonstrative alone, that does the pronoun's work, which is why it is catalogued here and these seats is catalogued with the determiners.
entries.variants: them ones (nonstandard — rural, Southern, and Appalachian American speech, and northern British) stacks the dialect them on top of the contested ones: Them ones ain't ripe yet.
entries.see also: this one / that one, these, those, them, ones, these (determiner)

entries.meaning: Picks out one countable thing from a set by pointing at it, with one standing in for the noun.
examples: Which folder do you want? — This one.
That one has a chip in the rim; take this one instead.
I've read this one twice and never got through that one.
Is it this one here, or that one on the end of the shelf?
That one was my grandmother's — the small blue one on the left.
Every apartment we looked at was too small, but this one has a second bedroom.
With a mass noun the prop-word drops out: ✓ This is the last of the coffee, ✗ this one of the coffee.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — one carries the stress; in that one the /t/ is normally unreleased or a glottal stop before the /w/, [ˌðæʔˈwʌn], which is why the two words sound welded together
entries.русский: этот, вот этот; тот — один конкретный предмет, выбранный из нескольких
entries.register: neutral — standard in speech and in writing, in every variety of English
entries.type: demonstrative + the prop-word one — a singular noun phrase with the noun left out
entries.person / number: third person singular
entries.refers to: one countable thing chosen out of a set already named or in view: Which folder? — This one. The prop-word needs a countable antecedent; with a mass noun English drops it and uses the bare demonstrative (✓ This is the last of the coffee, ✗ this one of the coffee). With people it is limited to the identifying frame the bare demonstrative allows, and it is blunter than the bare form — That one, in the blue jacket points a finger, where he, she, or a name is the ordinary choice.
entries.agreement: singular verb — This one fits. That one was broken when it came. The plural is bare these and those in edited prose, or these ones / those ones in speech.
entries.pattern: this one / that one as subject or object · [preposition] this one (in this one, with that one) · which one (the interrogative partner) · this one here, that one over there (the standard way to add the pointing that the dialect this here wedges inside the phrase) · this one … that one (contrastive pair) · the one that / the one we + relative clause
entries.contrast: Against bare this and that — the prop-word narrows the reference to a single countable item out of several. I'll take this can mean the pile, the deal, or the coffee; I'll take this one can only mean one item chosen from a set, which is why a store counter runs on this one. Against these ones / those ones — the singular is standard in American edited prose and the plural is not. Against the one — the one wants a defining clause behind it (the one you ordered), where this one does the defining by pointing. Against the determiner — this box, that folder keep the noun; one is precisely what stands in for it when the noun is dropped (this (determiner)).
entries.see also: these ones / those ones, this, that, one, ones, which, this (determiner)

entries.meaning: Stands in for a singular or uncountable noun just named, so that a comparison can be made without repeating the noun.
examples: The climate of Portland is much like that of northern Spain.
Her handwriting is neater than that of anyone else in the office.
The company's revenue now exceeds that of its former parent.
The tone of the second letter is nothing like that of the first.
A nonsmoker's risk is a small fraction of that of a pack-a-day smoker.
Its texture is closer to that of clay than to that of sand.
entries.pronunciation note: the /t/ flaps between vowels and of reduces — the phrase runs to [ˈðæɾəv], and in rapid speech to [ˈðæɾə]
entries.русский: у, чей — заменяет повторяемое сущ. ед. числа в сравнении: than that of X = чем у X
entries.register: formal to neutral; a written construction, rare in speech
entries.type: demonstrative pro-form (substitution for a repeated noun)
entries.person / number: third person singular; stands only for singular and uncountable nouns — the plural is those of
entries.refers to: a singular or uncountable noun already named in the same sentence, repeated without repeating the word: The climate of Portland is much like that of northern Spain (= the climate of northern Spain). It stands for things and abstractions. For a person, ordinary American English uses the possessive instead — than John's, not than that of John.
entries.agreement: the phrase heads a singular noun phrase, so any verb it governs is singular: That of the control group was unchanged. It does not affect the verb of the clause it sits in, which agrees with that clause's own subject.
entries.pattern: [noun] of X … than that of Y · like that of [noun phrase] · similar to that of · comparable to that of · that of the [noun] · a fraction of that of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The whole purpose of that of is to keep a comparison between like things. Leave it out and the sentence compares the wrong pair: ✗ Her salary is higher than a surgeon sets a salary against a person; ✓ higher than that of a surgeon, or, in plain American English, higher than a surgeon's. Number must match what is being replaced — singular that of, plural those of: ✗ Our returns beat that of our competitors → those of. Do not stack it on a possessive — ✗ that of Chicago's. And know the register — outside academic and technical prose the possessive or a simple repetition reads better, and that of in a short email sounds starched.
entries.see also: those of, that, that which, the same, the former, the latter

entries.meaning: Means "the thing that" — a formal written equivalent of what, chosen when a writer wants the weight of the demonstrative behind an abstraction.
examples: That which does not kill us makes us stronger.
We are remembered for that which we leave behind.
He spent thirty years chasing that which he could not name.
The audit separates that which can be verified from that which is merely asserted.
Keep that which is good, and let the rest go.
That which was promised in March has still not arrived.
entries.pronunciation note: both words keep full vowels; the stress falls on which
entries.русский: то, что — книжн., высокое; в современном языке обычно what
entries.case: none — the phrase takes whatever role its slot in the main clause assigns
entries.register: formal, literary, aphoristic; faintly archaic
entries.type: fused relative built on a demonstrative pronoun — it contains its own antecedent
entries.person / number: third person singular
entries.refers to: things and abstractions only, never people — that which means "the thing that." For people the parallel form is those who, or the dead he who of older prose. It takes no head noun and cannot be followed by one (✗ that which book); what follows is a relative clause.
entries.agreement: singular verb inside and out — That which remains is ours. The clause is singular even when its content is plural in sense: That which was promised has still not arrived.
entries.pattern: that which [relative clause] as subject · [verb] that which [relative clause] · [preposition] that which [relative clause] · all that which (rare, emphatic)
entries.contrast: Modern American English says what. What doesn't kill us and that which does not kill us are the same sentence in two registers, and the second is a stylistic choice, not a grammatical requirement. Use it for deliberate weight — proverbs, ceremonial prose, scripture-flavored writing — and not twice in a paragraph. Against those who: singular and non-human against plural and human. Against the plain relative that: the relative attaches to a noun that is already there (the thing that remains), while that which supplies the noun itself.
entries.see also: those which, those who, that, which, that which (determiner file)

entries.meaning: Stands in for a plural noun just named — or, with a personal pronoun, singles out the part of a group that a following clause describes.
examples: Our shipping costs are far below those of the national chains.
Her symptoms were identical to those of the earlier patients.
Those of you who registered online can skip the front desk.
Those of us who were there remember it differently.
The regulations are stricter than those of any neighboring state.
Only those of the applicants who submitted transcripts were considered.
entries.pronunciation note: of reduces to /əv/, and before a consonant often to /ə/ — those of us runs to [ˈðoʊzəvəs]
entries.русский: те, что у…; те из нас, из вас — замена мн. сущ. в сравнении и выделение части группы
entries.register: formal to neutral
entries.type: demonstrative pro-form (substitution for a repeated plural noun); also the partitive those of us / you / them
entries.person / number: third person plural — except that those of us and those of you pull first- and second-person agreement into the relative clause that follows
entries.refers to: two things. (1) A plural noun already named, repeated without repeating the word: Our margins are thinner than those of our competitors. (2) With a personal pronoun, a subset of a group that includes the speaker or the hearer: those of us who commute, those of you who registered online.
entries.agreement: plural throughout — Those of the samples that were contaminated have been discarded. In the partitive, the relative clause agrees with the pronoun after of: those of us who are on call, those of you who have questions — not ✗ those of us who is on call. The main verb is plural too: Those of us who work weekends get comp time.
entries.pattern: [plural noun] … than those of [noun phrase] · like those of / similar to those of · those of us / you / them + relative clause · those of the [plural noun] that/who [clause] · [preposition] those of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Number — plural those of against singular that of: ✗ scores higher than that of the other schools → those of the other schools. Form — the partitive idiom is those of us / those of you, fixed, whatever the distance involved; ✗ these of us and ✗ we of us are not English. Register — in ordinary American prose the possessive usually wins — our competitors' margins rather than the margins of our competitors or those of our competitors. And do not double the genitive: ✗ those of our competitors'.
entries.see also: that of, those, those who, those which

entries.meaning: Means "the ones that" — picks out a subset of things already in play and defines it by the clause that follows.
examples: Of the twelve proposals, we funded only those which had community backing.
Discard those that are cracked or warped.
The rule applies only to those which were signed before June.
I kept those that still fit and gave away the rest.
Those that pass inspection get a sticker on the base.
We are still missing those we ordered in April. (zero relative)
entries.pronunciation note: full vowels in both words; stress on which
entries.русский: те, которые — о предметах; книжн. вариант обычного those that
entries.register: formal (those which); neutral (those that)
entries.type: fused relative built on a demonstrative pronoun — the plural of that which
entries.person / number: third person plural
entries.refers to: things — a subset of a set already under discussion, defined by the relative clause that follows. It takes no head noun (✗ those which boxes). Those that stretches to people in careful prose, but those who is the normal choice there.
entries.agreement: plural in both clauses — Those which remain are damaged. Only those that pass inspection get a sticker.
entries.pattern: those which [relative clause] · those that [relative clause] · only those that [clause] · [preposition] those which [clause] · those + zero relative when the relative is the object of its clause (those we lost)
entries.contrast: Which against that. Those that is the everyday American form; those which sounds legal or literary, and in a restrictive clause an American copy editor will change which to that. That preference is a house convention rather than a rule of grammar — it will still be enforced on you in most American publishing. Dropping the relative. You may omit it only when it is the object of its clause: ✓ those we lost, ✗ those remain are damaged. People against things — those who for people and those which for things, with those that available for either — though with people those who is the normal choice.
entries.see also: that which, those who, those, which, those which (determiner file)

entries.meaning: Means "the people who" — names a group not by identity but by whatever the following clause says is true of them.
examples: Those who arrive after seven will be seated at intermission.
The fund exists for those who need it most.
Those who can, do; those who can't, teach.
Those of us who commute are used to the delays.
To those who wrote in with corrections: thank you.
He's one of those people who never answer email.
Those who disagreed said nothing at the time.
entries.pronunciation note: who keeps its full vowel here; the /h/ survives because the word is stressed
entries.русский: те, кто — только о людях и только с придаточным: those who wait «кто ждёт»
entries.case: none for those; the relative inside takes its own case (those who apply, formal those whom we hired)
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.type: fused relative built on a demonstrative pronoun
entries.person / number: third person plural — but those of us who takes first person plural agreement and those of you who second person
entries.refers to: people only, always plural, always with a relative clause behind it. Bare those names people only when it is identifying somebody in view (Those are my cousins); it cannot otherwise stand for "people," which is what the relative clause is here for. Who is the form for people, which for things, that for either, and whose for either as well (those whose names are called, a house whose roof leaks), so those who is the human member of the set and those which / those that the non-human one. It names a group by what is true of its members rather than by who they are, which is why it lives in rules, proverbs, and public announcements.
entries.agreement: plural verbs on both sides of the clause boundary — Those who wait are rewarded. Three traps. After those of us who, agreement is first person plural: those of us who are on call, ✗ who is. After those of you who, second person: those of you who have questions. And one of those … who takes a plural verb, because the clause describes the plural noun: He's one of those people who never answer email — the singular answers is common in speech and gets corrected in edited prose.
entries.pattern: those who [clause] + plural verb · [preposition] those who [clause] · those of us / you / them who [clause] · those whom [clause] (formal, relative as object) · those + reduced relative (those left behind, those responsible, those present)
entries.contrast: People against things — those who against those which / those that; who takes people, which takes things, that takes either, and whose takes either too (those whose applications are complete, the one building whose roof leaks) — English never developed a separate possessive for things, so whose covers both. Who against whom: the relative takes its own case inside the clause — those who apply (subject), those whom we hired (object) — but whom now survives mainly in the slot right after a preposition (those to whom we wrote, those with whom she worked). Everywhere else those who we hired is what Americans say and print, and only formal editing puts the m back. Register — those who apply early is a step up from people who apply early and two steps up from anybody who applies early — the demonstrative buys formality and loses warmth. Against the singular archaisms — he who, she who, they who are dead outside proverbs, and he who also reads as generic masculine, which is why those who has replaced it in American edited prose. Against the determiner — those people keeps the noun; those who replaces it.
entries.see also: those, those which, those of, that which, who, those who (determiner file)

entries.meaning: Points back at what is already written on the page — a passage, a table, or a list — rather than at anything in the world.
examples: The above is a summary of the position we took in March. (memo)
Please initial the above and return one copy to the office. (form)
Nothing in the above should be read as an admission of liability. (contract)
The above are the only exceptions the policy allows. (plural referent)
Which of these caused the outage? — All of the above. (the spoken idiom)
The foregoing applies to renewals as well as to new accounts. (variant)
In ordinary prose: That is a summary of the position we took in March.
entries.pronunciation note: the takes the /ði/ form used before a vowel, the one place its weak form changes shape instead of disappearing; the first syllable of above is the weak /ə/ and the stress falls on the second, and the phrase itself has no reduced form because it is barely ever said aloud
entries.русский: вышеизложенное, вышесказанное — юр., канц.; отсылка к месту выше в этом же тексте
entries.register: formal — legal, contractual, academic, and technical writing, and the multiple-choice test; almost never spoken except in the fixed all of the above
entries.type: text-pointing (anaphoric) pro-form — the plus an adverb of place, used as a noun phrase
entries.person / number: third person; number comes from what it stands for — singular for one passage or statement, plural for a list of items
entries.refers to: the material already on the page — a passage, a paragraph, a table, a list, or a statement printed earlier in the same document. The metaphor is the page read from the top down, and it is the whole of the word's meaning here: above means "earlier in this document," not "higher up" and not "over there." It reaches people only through something already written (the above are hereby notified, legal drafting, where the reader has to go up the page to learn who they are).
entries.agreement: the verb follows the referent, not the phrase — The above is a summary of our position (one passage) against The above are the only exceptions the policy allows (a list of items). Neither is more correct than the other; what decides is whether the writer is pointing at one block of text or at several things in it.
entries.pattern: the above as subject · [preposition] the above (nothing in the above) · [verb] the above (initial the above, see the above) · all of the above / none of the above (the multiple-choice idiom, and the one use that reached ordinary speech) · as noted above, as stated above (the adverb, far commoner than the pronoun) · the above-mentioned, the above-named (determiners in practice — they lean on a noun)
entries.contrast: Against the following — direction on the page, and nothing else: the above points back, the following points forward. Against this and that — the demonstratives point at ideas in a conversation and are the ordinary choice everywhere outside a document; the above in an email reads as a memo written by a lawyer, and this or that almost always does the job better. Against the determiner — the above table, the above-mentioned clause, and the aforementioned exception all sit on a noun and are catalogued in the determiner dictionary; only the bare standalone the above is a pronoun. The one living idiom — all of the above escaped the multiple-choice test and is now ordinary American speech for "every one of them" (What went wrong? — All of the above), and none of the above has gone the same way, onto ballots and into political commentary.
entries.variants: the foregoing (formal, chiefly legal and academic, and pointing at a whole preceding stretch rather than a spot: The foregoing is subject to change without notice); the aforementioned and the aforesaid (legal, and far commoner as determiners — the aforesaid tenant); the above-mentioned and the above-named (determiners); British legal writing adds the undermentioned, which an American meets only in imported documents. Every one of them is heavier than this, and none belongs in ordinary prose.
entries.see also: the following, the foregoing, the aforementioned, the former, the last-mentioned, that, this, the same, aforementioned (determiner), aforesaid (determiner)

entries.meaning: Points back at a person, a party, or a document already named earlier in the same document — the draftsman's way of not writing the name twice.
examples: The aforementioned shall have thirty days from the date of service in which to respond. (court filing)
Liability for damage to the aforementioned rests with the lessee. (lease)
The aforementioned are jointly and severally liable under Section 4. (plural referent — several parties)
Nothing in this rider limits the coverage described for the aforementioned. (insurance)
The aforesaid is void if the property changes hands before closing. (variant, and the commoner bare form)
Determiner use, and the ordinary one: the aforementioned clause was struck at closing.
In plain English: That clause was struck at closing.
entries.pronunciation note: the takes the /ði/ form used before a vowel; the main stress falls on -men- and a secondary one on -fore-, and the ending is the reduced /ʃənd/. Five syllables with nothing to shorten, which is part of why the phrase never left the page
entries.русский: вышеупомянутый — юр.; о лице или предмете, уже названном ранее в документе
entries.register: formal and legal — contracts, leases, insurance policies, statutes, briefs, patent claims, and the occasional academic footnote; in speech it is either a lawyer at work or a joke
entries.type: text-pointing (anaphoric) pro-form — a participial adjective standing as a whole noun phrase
entries.person / number: third person; number comes from the referent — singular for one item or one party, plural for several (The aforementioned are jointly liable)
entries.refers to: a person, a party, an item, or a document already named earlier in the same document, pointed at without being named a second time. That is what separates it from its neighbors: the foregoing sweeps up a whole preceding stretch of text and the above points at a place on the page, while the aforementioned points at one identified thing wherever it was introduced. It is also the one page-pointing phrase in this file that reaches people freely, because the parties to a contract are exactly what a draftsman keeps having to re-name.
entries.agreement: the verb follows the referent, not the phrase — The aforementioned is attached as Exhibit B (one document) against The aforementioned are hereby notified (several parties). Where an American actually meets it: signing a lease, reading an insurance rider, or being served with a court filing.
entries.pattern: the aforementioned as subject (the aforementioned shall be liable) · [verb] the aforementioned · [preposition] the aforementioned (in the aforementioned, for the aforementioned) · none of the aforementioned · the aforementioned + [noun] (the aforementioned clause, the aforementioned defendant) — the determiner use, and far the commoner one, catalogued in the determiner dictionary
entries.contrast: Against the above — a location on the page against a thing already introduced. Against the foregoing — one named item against the whole passage in front of it. Against the former, the latter, and the last-mentioned — those count position in a list, and this one does not count at all; it simply says "the one I already named." The determiner is the real word — nearly every occurrence in the wild has the noun present, and the bare pronoun is confined to drafting. Register warning — outside a legal document it reads as parody, and the American plain-English drafting movement has spent fifty years cutting it out of contracts; in ordinary prose write this, that, or the noun itself.
entries.variants: the aforesaid (the commonest legal sibling, and the one that still turns up bare — the aforesaid shall be void); the aforenamed and the above-named, used chiefly of parties; the said (the said tenant), a determiner and the most heavily marked legalism of the set; the undersigned, the drafting phrase for whoever signs, which behaves the same way and is treated with the archaic, literary, and dialectal pronouns.
entries.see also: the above, the foregoing, the following, the last-mentioned, that, the aforesaid, the aforementioned (as legal style), the undersigned, aforementioned (determiner), aforesaid (determiner)

entries.meaning: Points forward at what comes next in the document — the list, the names, or the terms about to be given.
examples: The following are eligible to vote in the September election:
The following is the text of the resolution as amended.
Please read the following carefully before you sign anything.
Complete the following and return it with your deposit.
The following have been promoted, effective Monday: Ruiz, Delgado, and Park.
The payment terms are as follows: thirty days net, two percent for ten. (frozen — never ✗ as follow)
Business email: Please review the below and confirm. (edited prose: the following, or this)
entries.pronunciation note: the is the ordinary weak /ðə/ before the consonant; following keeps its first-syllable stress, and in running speech the -ing reduces to /ɪn/ and the middle vowel weakens to /ə/ with a linking /w/ — [ˈfɑləwɪn]
entries.русский: нижеследующее — то, что идёт дальше в тексте, обычно сразу после двоеточия
entries.register: formal to neutral — documents, instructions, agendas, announcements, and rosters; ordinary in business writing and rare in speech
entries.type: text-pointing (cataphoric) pro-form — the forward-pointing partner of the above
entries.person / number: third person; number comes from what is about to be given — one passage or a list
entries.refers to: what comes next in the document: the list, the passage, the names, or the terms about to be set out, usually right after a colon. Like the above it lives on the page and dies in speech. It is the one page-pointing phrase that reaches people freely, because the list after the colon is so often a list of names — The following have been promoted, effective Monday:
entries.agreement: the verb takes the number of what actually follows — The following is the text of the resolution (one thing) against The following are eligible to vote (several). Both are right; the mistake is picking one out of habit and then contradicting it with the list. Note that The following is a list of the eligible voters is singular for a good reason: what follows is one list.
entries.pattern: The following + [verb] + colon · [verb] the following (consider the following, complete the following) · [preposition] the following · as follows (frozen: The terms are as follows:) · the below (business email — see Variants)
entries.contrast: Against the above — direction on the page. Against this — pointing forward at something not yet said is exactly what this does in speech (Listen to this:), and the following is what a document does instead; the two are the same gesture in two registers. As follows never inflects — it is an old impersonal construction, frozen singular however many items come after it: ✓ The rules are as follows, ✗ as follow. Against the determiner — the following morning, the following items lean on a noun and are catalogued with the determiners under subsequent, following; only the standalone use is a pronoun.
entries.variants: the below (Please review the below and confirm) is corporate email English. It is spreading fast in American business writing and is still marked wrong by editors, on the grammatical ground that below had no noun use to begin with — write the following, the text below, or plain this. The British legal the undermentioned covers the same ground and is rare in the United States.
entries.see also: the above, the foregoing, the aforementioned, the latter, this, so, subsequent, following (determiner)

entries.meaning: Points back at the whole of what has just been written — a paragraph, a section, or a run of recitals taken as one block.
examples: The foregoing is subject to change without notice. (contract)
Notwithstanding the foregoing, the tenant may terminate on sixty days' written notice. (the standard drafting frame)
Nothing in the foregoing creates a partnership between the parties.
The foregoing are the only warranties the manufacturer gives. (plural referent — a list)
None of the foregoing shall be deemed employees of the company. (people, reached through the text)
The foregoing summarizes the argument of Chapters 2 through 4. (academic)
Not this word: forgoing the bonus meant a smaller tax bill. (= giving up)
entries.pronunciation note: the is the ordinary weak /ðə/ before the consonant, and the compound takes its main stress on fore-, which is the whole difference between it and the verb forgoing /fɔrˈgoʊɪŋ/; nothing in the phrase reduces, because in the one register that uses it nothing is said quickly
entries.русский: вышеизложенное — книжн., юр.; всё сказанное выше целиком, а не отдельный пункт
entries.register: formal — contracts, statutes, board resolutions, briefs, and academic prose; effectively never spoken
entries.type: text-pointing (anaphoric) pro-form — a participial adjective standing as a whole noun phrase
entries.person / number: third person; number comes from the referent — usually singular, because what it points at is one block of text, but plural when the block is a list
entries.refers to: the whole of what has just been written — the preceding sentence, paragraph, section, or run of recitals, taken as one lump rather than pinned to a spot. That sweep is the difference between it and its neighbors: the above names a place on the page, the aforementioned names one item already introduced, and the foregoing takes in everything up to here. It reaches people only through the text, and only in drafting (none of the foregoing shall be deemed employees).
entries.agreement: the verb follows what the writer is pointing at — The foregoing is a summary and does not constitute legal advice (one passage) against The foregoing are the only warranties given (a list of items). Neither is more correct than the other; the mistake is choosing one and then contradicting it later in the same sentence.
entries.pattern: The foregoing + [verb] · notwithstanding the foregoing (much the commonest frame in American contract drafting) · nothing in the foregoing · none of the foregoing · subject to the foregoing · the foregoing paragraph, the foregoing provisions (the determiner use, which needs a noun)
entries.contrast: Against the above — the direction is the same and the scope is not: the above is a location, the foregoing is everything preceding. Against the following — backward against forward. Against the aforementioned — a whole passage against a single named party or document. Against forgoing — one letter and one stressed syllable apart, and a completely different word: the foregoing means "what came before," while forgoing means "giving up" (forgoing the bonus). No American spell-checker catches the swap, and it is a standing embarrassment in contract drafts. Register — notwithstanding the foregoing is a genuine term of art and has survived every plain-English campaign aimed at it, but bare the foregoing in an email is a lawyer's tic; write this, the above, or the name of the thing.
entries.variants: the preceding (the preceding applies to renewals as well) is the plainer academic sibling and carries much less register cost; the premises, in the old legal sense of "the matters just recited," covers the same ground in a contract's recitals (in consideration of the premises) and nowhere else; British drafting adds the aforegoing, which an American meets only in imported documents.
entries.see also: the above, the aforementioned, the following, the last-mentioned, that, the foregoing (as legal style), the premises, aforementioned (determiner)

entries.meaning: Stands for the first of exactly two things just named, in the order they were named.
examples: We can fly or drive; the former is faster, but the latter is cheaper.
She has a law degree and an MBA; the former has been the more useful of the two.
Of the two designs, the former came in under budget.
Both the sedan and the wagon are on the lot, and I'd take the former.
The report blames the weather and the contractor. The former is nobody's fault.
Not this word: her former husband, the former president. (adjective, = previous)
Plain American: We can fly or drive, and flying is faster.
entries.pronunciation note: the is the ordinary weak /ðə/; former takes the stress and keeps the r-colored /ɚ/ of General American, and has no weak form of its own
entries.русский: первый (из двух) — первое из двух только что названных; ровно двух, не больше
entries.register: formal to neutral; a written device, uncommon in speech
entries.type: text-pointing pro-form of order — the first of exactly two things just named
entries.person / number: third person; it takes the number of the noun it stands for — The former is cheaper, The former were imported
entries.refers to: the first of exactly two things named just before it, counted in the order they were named and not by distance, recency, or importance. Two is a hard limit: with three items the pair has nothing to hang on, and the repair is to name the thing (oak is cheapest) or to write the first. It stands for things, ideas, places, and — in careful writing — people, though repeating the person's name is friendlier to the reader.
entries.agreement: singular or plural according to the referent — Of the two proposals, the former is cheaper; Of the two crews, the former have worked together before is possible, though American English normally treats a collective as singular (the former has worked together before).
entries.pattern: the former … the latter (the pair, always in that order) · of the two, the former · the former + [verb] · [preposition] the former (in the former, for the former) · the former of the two · the former … the latter … with a semicolon between the halves
entries.contrast: Against the latter — order of mention, nothing else. Against this and that — in older prose that sometimes marks the first-mentioned and this the second, on the logic that the first is further back in the text; almost no modern American reader parses that, and former/latter says it outright. Against the adjective former — her former husband, the former president, the former Soviet Union mean "previous," a completely different word that sits on a noun and belongs with the determiners (former, latter). The readability trap — the pair forces the reader back up the sentence to count, and Chicago and Garner both advise repeating the noun whenever the antecedents are more than a line away, or whenever the two items are not plainly parallel. Two only — ✗ We looked at oak, maple, and cherry; the former is cheapest.
entries.variants: the first is the plain American alternative and carries no register cost (the first is cheaper); the one … the other does the same work when the point is contrast rather than counting.
entries.see also: the latter, the last-mentioned, the above, the following, that of, former, latter (determiner)

entries.meaning: Stands for whichever item in a list was named most recently — the phrase that takes over from the latter once there are more than two.
examples: Of the three statutes, the last-mentioned was repealed in 1998.
The estate went to a brother, two cousins, and a charity, and the last-mentioned declined the bequest.
She cited Holmes, Brandeis, and Cardozo, and quoted the last-mentioned at length.
Copper, aluminum, and steel were all tested, and the last-mentioned failed at the lowest load.
The first-mentioned of the four defendants has since settled. (the partner form)
Where the items are people, legal writing prefers the -named form: the last-named was called as a witness.
Plain American: of the three, the last is the most expensive.
entries.pronunciation note: the is the ordinary weak /ðə/; the compound takes its main stress on last and a secondary one on -men-, the ordinary American pattern for a hyphenated compound, and neither half has a weak form
entries.русский: последний из упомянутых — юр., книжн.; при перечне любой длины, в отличие от the latter
entries.register: formal — legal drafting, academic and technical prose, and reference writing; not spoken
entries.type: text-pointing pro-form of order — the item named most recently, in a list of any length
entries.person / number: third person; it takes the number of what it stands for — The last-mentioned is the cheapest, The last-mentioned were withdrawn
entries.refers to: whichever item in a preceding list was named last, counted by order of mention and by nothing else — not by distance, recency in time, or importance. Its whole reason to exist is the two-item limit on the latter: with three or more items the latter is an error, and this is the phrase that takes over. It stands for things, statutes, cases, and materials, and in legal and biographical writing for people as well (the last-mentioned was called as a witness).
entries.agreement: singular or plural according to the referent — Of the three statutes, the last-mentioned was repealed in 1998; Of the four groups surveyed, the last-mentioned were the least likely to respond. The phrase itself never inflects: there is no ✗ the last-mentioneds and no comparative.
entries.pattern: of the three / four / five …, the last-mentioned · the last-mentioned + [verb] · [preposition] the last-mentioned · the first-mentioned … the last-mentioned (the pair, for a list of three or more) · the last-mentioned + [noun] (the last-mentioned case) — the determiner use · the last-named, the first-named (the forms preferred when the items are people)
entries.contrast: Against the latter — the count, and nothing else. The latter means the second of exactly two and is simply wrong with three; the last-mentioned means the most recent of any number, and it is available with two as well, though it sounds heavy there. Against the former — the same relation at the other end of the list, where the partner form is the first-mentioned. Against the last — plain the last is the everyday American alternative and costs nothing in register: of the three, the last is the most expensive. Against the adjective last — last week, the last person to leave mean "final" or "most recent in time," where the counting here is over mentions on the page. The readability trap, doubled — the former/latter pair already sends the reader back up the sentence to count, and a list of five makes it worse; Chicago and Garner both advise naming the thing instead, and with anything longer than a short parallel list they are plainly right.
entries.variants: the first-mentioned, the other end of the list (the first-mentioned of the four has since settled); the last-named and the first-named, which legal and biographical writing prefers when the items are people; the last and the first, the plain American forms. British drafting writes the lastmentioned solid and the last mentioned open; American editing hyphenates.
entries.see also: the latter, the former, the above, the aforementioned, the foregoing, former, latter (determiner)

entries.meaning: Stands for the second of exactly two things just named, in the order they were named.
examples: We can fly or drive; the former is faster, and the latter is cheaper.
He was offered Denver or Tulsa, and he took the latter.
Of the two witnesses, the latter is the one the jury believed.
The bill covers highways and bridges, and the latter got most of the money.
She writes fiction and criticism; the latter pays better and the former sells better.
Watch the vowel: ✗ the later of the two → the latter of the two.
Three items take the last: oak, maple, and cherry — the last is the most expensive.
entries.pronunciation note: the /t/ between vowels is the ordinary American flap, so most Americans make latter and ladder sound alike; the is the weak /ðə/, and latter itself never reduces
entries.русский: второй, последний (из двух) — второе из двух только что названных
entries.register: formal to neutral; a written device, uncommon in speech
entries.type: text-pointing pro-form of order — the second of exactly two things just named
entries.person / number: third person; it takes the number of the noun it stands for
entries.refers to: the second of exactly two things named just before it, counted in the order of mention. With three or more the word is the last, not the latter. Like its partner it stands for things and ideas freely and for people only in careful writing.
entries.agreement: singular or plural according to the referent — Of the two bids, the latter was withdrawn; Of the two teams, the latter are unbeaten (British-leaning) against the ordinary American the latter is unbeaten.
entries.pattern: the former … the latter · of the two, the latter · the latter + [verb] · [preposition] the latter · the latter two, the latter three (postdeterminer — "the last two of the group," a different job) · the latter half, the latter part of the year (determiner use)
entries.contrast: Against the former — order of mention. Against later — the two words differ by one vowel, /ˈlæɾɚ/ against /ˈleɪɾɚ/, and ✗ the later of the two is a common American slip for the latter of the two: later means "further on in time," latter means "the second of two." Against the last — three or more items take the last, or the formal the last-mentioned, and the latter with a three-item list is an error, not a stretch. Against the determiner and postdeterminer uses — the latter half of the year and the latter two candidates both lean on a noun; only the bare standalone form is the pronoun. The readability trap is the same as its partner's: if the reader has to go back and count, name the thing instead.
entries.variants: the second (plain American: the second is cheaper); the other when there are two and the first has already been dealt with.
entries.see also: the former, the last-mentioned, the above, the following, that of, former, latter (determiner)

entries.meaning: Stands in for a whole statement just made or plainly implied — "that very thing."
examples: He never admitted it outright, but he said as much to the auditors.
So you knew the deal was dead? — I thought as much.
The memo says as much, in the second paragraph.
She told me as much the day she resigned.
If the numbers are wrong, the footnote will say as much.
As much was clear from the first week. (formal, fronted)
Not the pro-form: We spent as much as they did. (a comparison of quantity)
entries.pronunciation note: as is nearly always the weak /əz/ here and can devoice to /əs/ after a voiceless consonant; much carries the stress, so I thought as much runs to [aɪˈθɔɾəzˈmʌtʃ] with the /t/ of thought flapped
entries.русский: именно это, так и — заменяет целое высказывание: I thought as much «так я и думал»
entries.register: neutral to formal; confined to a short list of fixed frames
entries.type: pro-form standing for a whole clause or proposition (a pro-clause), demonstrative in force
entries.person / number: invariant — no person, number, or gender
entries.refers to: the proposition just stated, or one plainly implied — "that, that very thing." I thought as much means "that is what I thought," and He said as much means "that is what he said, in so many words." What it points at is always a whole statement, never a noun: ✗ I'll take as much in the pointing sense is not English, though it is a perfectly good quantity phrase in a comparison.
entries.agreement: almost none of its own. It is nearly always a complement rather than a subject, and it governs no verb — ✗ As much surprised me → That surprised me. The one exception is the formal fronted frame As much was clear from the start, where it is the subject and the verb is singular.
entries.pattern: I thought as much · [verb of saying] + as much (he said as much, she admitted as much, the report says as much, he told me as much) · as much was clear from the start (formal, and the one frame in which it fronts) · not this construction — as much as + [noun phrase or clause] (comparison — we paid as much as they did; concession — as much as I'd like to)
entries.contrast: Against so — the same job for a smaller set of verbs. I think so is idiomatic and ✗ I think as much is not; He said so and He said as much are both good, with as much the more formal and carrying "and now it is confirmed"; and I thought as much is the fixed phrase, where I thought so is the plainer everyday version of it. Against that — that is a full noun phrase and can head a clause as its subject (That surprised me); as much is neither a noun phrase you can move around freely nor a possible subject. Against the comparative as much as — the tell is what comes after: the pro-form takes nothing (He said as much.), while the comparison demands a second term (He paid as much as she did). Against as such — a different phrase doing a different job, "in that capacity" (see such).
entries.see also: so, not, such, the same, this much / that much, ditto, that

entries.meaning: Seconds what was just said, or marks a line in a list as a repeat of the line above it.
examples: I'm skipping the Friday call. — Ditto.
The first-quarter numbers were revised, and ditto the second quarter's.
He hates the new logo, and ditto for the tagline.
She thinks the deadline is unrealistic. Ditto half the department.
In the ledger each repeated address is marked with a ditto rather than typed out again.
Ditto that — I wouldn't sign it either. (conversational)
In a report, write: The same is true of the second quarter.
entries.pronunciation note: the /t/ between the vowels flaps in ordinary American speech — [ˈdɪɾoʊ] — and the stress is on the first syllable; no weak form, since the word is normally a whole utterance by itself
entries.русский: то же самое — разг.; в столбцах и списках заменяется знаком повтора 〃
entries.register: informal in speech; in writing a list-and-ledger convention, where the ditto mark 〃 does the work instead
entries.type: pro-form of identity — "the same again"; from Tuscan Italian ditto "said," taken into English in the 1620s as a bookkeeper's word
entries.person / number: invariant, and always singular in force
entries.refers to: what was just said or just written, without repeating it — in a column, the entry directly above; in conversation, the whole of the other speaker's statement, which the speaker is seconding. It is also a verb (He dittoed my objection) and a noun (the ditto marks), and neither of those is a pronoun.
entries.agreement: none of its own. In the reply use it is a whole utterance and takes no verb, and in Ditto for the second quarter it heads a fragment; there is no ✗ Ditto is true of the second quarter, which needs the same.
entries.pattern: Ditto. (bare reply, seconding) · Ditto for [noun phrase] · Ditto that (American conversational) · and ditto [noun phrase] (the first quarter was revised, and ditto the second) · the ditto mark 〃 (or a pair of straight quotes) under a repeated line in a list or ledger
entries.contrast: Against same here — identical work in the same register, and Same here is the commoner American reply; ditto now carries a light jokiness that same here does not. Against the same — the same is a full noun phrase and takes a verb (The same is true of the other branches); ditto is a fragment and cannot (✗ Ditto is true of the other branches). Against likewise — likewise is the one of the three that survives in formal writing (Likewise, the second clause was struck); ditto in a report reads as a lapse, and the fix is the same. Not the duplicating machine — the ditto an American over fifty remembers from grade school, and the purple-smelling sheets that came off it, is a trademark for a spirit duplicator and has nothing to do with the pronoun beyond the shared idea of copying.
entries.see also: the same, one and the same, as much, so, such

entries.meaning: Stands in for a whole clause and negates it in the same breath — the negative half of the pair whose affirmative half is so.
examples: Is the meeting cancelled? — I hope not.
Will we get the deposit back? — I'm afraid not.
Did anybody call while I was out? — I guess not.
Are you planning to argue with her about it? — I think not. (clipped and formal; the everyday negative is I don't think so)
If not, we'll have to move the whole week.
Certainly not — I never agreed to any of that.
Wrong pattern with this verb: ✗ I don't hope so → I hope not.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form in this use — the pro-clause not is the stressed word in its answer and keeps the full open /ɑ/ of General American, I hope not [aɪˈhoʊpˈnɑt]; the clitic n't of don't and isn't is the reduced negator and belongs to a different construction, and the two never trade places
entries.русский: нет — заменяет отрицаемое предложение целиком: I hope not «надеюсь, что нет»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: negative pro-clause — the negative counterpart of so
entries.person / number: invariant — no person, number, or gender
entries.refers to: the negation of a whole clause just stated or plainly in the air, never a noun. Is the flight cancelled? — I hope not means I hope that it is not cancelled, and the pronoun it cannot stand in its place (✗ I hope it, ✗ I'm afraid it). What it points at is the same kind of thing so points at — a proposition — with the sign flipped.
entries.agreement: none of its own. It is a complement, never a subject, and it governs no verb: ✗ Not surprised me → That didn't surprise me. The verb in front of it agrees with that verb's own subject.
entries.pattern: [verb of hoping, guessing, or saying] + not (I hope not, I'm afraid not, I guess not, I suppose not, she says not) · I think not (formal and clipped) · if not · why not · certainly not, absolutely not, of course not (bare replies) · whether or not · not this construction — the clitic negator of I don't think so, which negates the verb and leaves so to carry the clause
entries.contrast: Which verbs take not and which push the negative onto the main verb is the whole difficulty, and the two lists barely overlap. Verbs that take not: hope, guess, be afraid, say, suspect — I hope not, I'm afraid not, I guess not — and for these the other pattern does not exist at all: ✗ I don't hope so is not English. Verbs that push the negative onto the verb instead — think, believe, suppose, imagine, expect — I don't think so is the ordinary American negative, and I think not survives only as a clipped, faintly starchy retort. Against so: exact counterparts filling the same slot after the same verbs, which is why the two are learned together. Against the ordinary adverb not: He is not coming negates a verb inside a clause that is fully present; the pro-clause not replaces the clause outright, which is why it can be a whole answer by itself. Against no: No answers the question and stops; I hope not answers it and says how the speaker feels about the answer.
entries.see also: so, as much, this much / that much, that, such

entries.meaning: Says that two things named separately have turned out to be a single thing.
examples: The complaining neighbor and the landlord turned out to be one and the same.
For our purposes, the invoice number and the order number are one and the same.
Style and substance are not one and the same.
She wrote under three names, and no critic guessed that all three were one and the same.
The company that filed the patent and the company that sued over it were one and the same.
With the noun spelled out: they were one and the same person.
Looser, and weaker: to him, Saturday and Sunday are one and the same.
entries.pronunciation note: and reduces to /ən/ or to a syllabic /n/ and the to the weak /ðə/, so the middle of the phrase all but disappears — [ˌwʌnən(d)ðəˈseɪm] — and the stress lands on same
entries.русский: одно и то же лицо, один и тот же — усиленное the same, требует двух названных предметов
entries.register: neutral; a set phrase, equally at home in speech and in writing
entries.type: emphatic pro-form of identity — an intensified the same
entries.person / number: invariant, and singular in force: it says that two names or descriptions have turned out to have exactly one referent
entries.refers to: two things or people already named, asserted to be a single one — The complaining neighbor and the landlord were one and the same. It points back at both of the noun phrases in front of it at once, which is why it needs two of them: ✗ He is one and the same, with nothing for him to be the same as, is not a sentence.
entries.agreement: it follows be, and the subject is coordinate or plural, so the verb is plural — The two accounts are one and the same; The author and the translator were one and the same. The phrase itself never changes shape: there is no ✗ ones and the same and no comparative.
entries.pattern: [coordinate subject] + be + one and the same · X and Y are one and the same · are not one and the same (the negative — the commonest use of all, because the phrase belongs to argument) · one and the same person / thing / man (with the noun spelled out, which makes it a determiner phrase rather than the bare pronoun)
entries.contrast: Against the same — the same matches a new instance to an old one (She ordered the salmon and I'll have the same); one and the same collapses two descriptions into a single referent (the pen name and the professor were one and the same). Against identical — identical allows two objects that match, and one and the same allows only one object with two names. That is the whole distinction arguments turn on: two identical keys are two keys, one and the same key is one. Against the selfsame — the literary determiner (the selfsame afternoon), which needs a noun behind it (selfsame). The empty use — in loose speech it sometimes means only "much alike" (To him, Tuesday and Wednesday are one and the same), which is understood everywhere and quietly throws away the distinction the phrase exists to make.
entries.see also: the same, ditto, such, same (determiner), selfsame (determiner)

entries.meaning: Stands in for a whole clause that has just been said or is obvious from the situation, so the speaker does not have to repeat it.
examples: Is the meeting still on? — I think so.
I hope so, but I wouldn't count on it.
I told you so.
If so, we'll need a bigger room.
She said so herself, in front of the whole committee.
Anyone wishing to appeal must do so within thirty days.
Is it going to rain all week? — I'm afraid so.
He's late again. — So I see.

senses.head: Pro-clause after verbs of thinking and saying
body: Do you think it will rain? — I think so. The commonest use by far, and the one that has to be learned verb by verb.

senses.head: "Do so" — replacing a verb phrase
body: Formal and written: Employees may park in Lot C; those who do so must display a permit. In speech, do it or do that.

senses.head: "If so"
body: A whole conditional clause compressed to two words: Are you driving? If so, I'll ride with you.

senses.head: Confirming what someone has said
body: So it seems. So I hear. So they say. The pro-form points back at the other speaker's sentence.

senses.head: Inversion after so, meaning "the same is true of"
body: I'm exhausted. — So am I. The negative counterpart is neither: I don't drive. — Neither do I.
examples: Is the meeting still on? — I think so.
I hope so, but I wouldn't count on it.
I told you so.
If so, we'll need a bigger room.
She said so herself, in front of the whole committee.
Anyone wishing to appeal must do so within thirty days.
Is it going to rain all week? — I'm afraid so.
He's late again. — So I see.

entries.pronunciation note: unstressed but not reduced — the diphthong survives, and I think so runs to [aɪˈθɪŋk soʊ]; the word has no weak form at all
entries.русский: так, да, это — заменяет целое предложение: I think so «думаю, да»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: pro-form standing for a whole clause (pro-clause), demonstrative in origin
entries.person / number: invariant — no person, number, or gender
entries.refers to: a whole clause or proposition, just stated or obvious from the situation — never a noun. Is it raining? — I think so means I think that it is raining. Because it stands for a clause and not a noun phrase, it cannot take its place: ✗ I hope it, ✗ I'm afraid it.
entries.agreement: none of its own — it is not a subject and never governs a verb; the verb in front of it agrees with that verb's own subject.
entries.pattern: [verb of thinking or saying] + so (I think so, I hope so, I guess so, I suppose so, I'm afraid so, I told you so, She said so) · if so · do so (replacing a whole verb phrase) · so + inversion (So do I, So it seems) · more so, even more so
entries.contrast: Which verbs take it, and how each one is negated, is the entire difficulty. Verbs that take so: think, believe, suppose, expect, imagine, hope, guess, say, tell (someone), be afraid, seem, appear, hear. Verbs that do not: know (✗ I know so → I know), doubt (✗ I doubt so → I doubt it), be sure (→ I'm sure of it). Two negative patterns, not interchangeable: with think, believe, suppose, imagine, expect, the negative goes on the main verb — I don't think so (the formal I think not survives, barely); with hope, guess, be afraid, say, the negative is not — I hope not, I'm afraid not, and ✗ I don't hope so is not English. Against that: that replaces a clause as a full noun phrase and can be a subject (That surprised me); so cannot be a subject (✗ So surprised me) and only follows certain verbs.
entries.see also: not, such, the same, as much, this much / that much, that, this

entries.meaning: Points back at the kind of thing or the state of affairs just described — "that, and that sort of thing."
examples: Such is life.
Such was the plan, at least until the funding fell through.
He was elected treasurer and, as such, signs every check.
The house, such as it is, has been in the family a hundred years.
Such were his last words to the committee.
We stocked pens, paper, tape, and such. (informal)
The document is a draft and should be read as such.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /sətʃ/ whenever it is unstressed, which is most of the time in running speech
entries.русский: таков, такое — книжн.: Such was the outcome «таков был итог»; as such «как таковой»
entries.register: formal to literary as a pronoun — the determiner such a mess is ordinary, the standalone pronoun is not; and such is informal; bare such in legal drafting is archaic
entries.type: demonstrative pro-form meaning "of that kind, that"
entries.person / number: invariant; the referent may be singular or plural, and the verb follows the referent, not the pronoun
entries.refers to: a kind of thing, or a state of affairs, just described: Such was the outcome (= that was the outcome, and that is what it was like). In as such it refers to the capacity or description just named — He is the ranking officer and will be treated as such. It reaches people only through a description, never by pointing at one.
entries.agreement: in the fronted pattern the verb agrees with the real subject, which follows it: Such is life. Such were his last words. Such was the case in every office we visited. Matching the verb to such instead of to the real subject (✗ Such was his last words) is the standard error here.
entries.pattern: such + [verb] + [subject] (Such is life, Such was the plan) · as such · such as it is / such as they are · and such (informal, = and the like) · such as a bare pronoun in legal drafting (notify the tenant, and such shall have ten days to respond)
entries.contrast: Against the determiner such: the determiner leans on a noun (such a mess, such nonsense), the pronoun stands alone (Such is life).
