Against so: so stands for a clause and follows a verb (I think so); such stands for a kind and usually sits in front of the verb (Such was the plan). Against that: that names the thing, such characterizes it — That was the outcome identifies, Such was the outcome says what sort of outcome it was. The as such trap: it means "in that capacity" or "strictly speaking," not "therefore." He is the executor and, as such, signs the checks ✓. The vendor missed the deadline; as such, we cancelled is common in American business writing and is still marked wrong by careful editors — write therefore or so.
entries.see also: so, the same, such and such, the like, that, such (determiner)

entries.meaning: Holds a slot open for a name, date, or amount the speaker will not supply — a deliberate blank.
examples: They tell you the fee is such and such, and then the paperwork adds another fifty.
He kept saying he served from such and such to such and such, and the dates never matched.
You fill in such-and-such on line 12 and the form does the rest.
It's always the same story: the check went out on such and such and the bank lost it.
Don't tell me it costs such and such — give me the number.
Determiner use, and the commoner one: be at such-and-such a gate by such-and-such a time.
For a person: Mr. So-and-so from the front office signed off on it.
entries.pronunciation note: and reduces to /ən/ or to a syllabic /n/ and the first such weakens to /sətʃ/, so the phrase runs to [ˌsətʃn̩ˈsʌtʃ] with the stress on the second such
entries.русский: такой-то — заполнитель вместо намеренно не названных имени, даты, суммы
entries.register: informal to neutral; chiefly spoken, and written such-and-such with hyphens
entries.type: pro-form standing for something the speaker is deliberately declining to name — a placeholder, not a pointer
entries.person / number: invariant, and treated as singular
entries.refers to: a name, a date, a place, or an amount that the speaker is leaving blank on purpose, for the hearer to fill in with whatever the real case turns out to be: They tell you the fee is such and such, and then the paperwork adds fifty dollars. It points at nothing — that is the point of it — which makes it the odd member of this file: every other entry here has an antecedent. For people the partner form is so-and-so.
entries.agreement: singular verb — Such-and-such is always the excuse. There is no plural and no possessive.
entries.pattern: [verb or preposition] + such and such (do such and such, at such and such, from such and such to such and such) · such-and-such a [noun] (the determiner use — at such-and-such a time — and much the commoner one; see the determiner dictionary) · Mr. So-and-so (the person-shaped partner) · thus and so (dated)
entries.contrast: Against such — plain such points back at a kind of thing just described (Such was the plan); the doubled such and such points at nothing at all and holds a slot open. Against whatever and whatnot — those wave away the rest of a list; such and such keeps one slot empty and specific-shaped. Against so-and-so — things and quantities against people, and note that so-and-so has a second life as a mild American euphemism for a person you are not going to name politely (the old so-and-so). The determiner is commoner — most real occurrences are such-and-such a time, such-and-such a form, with the noun present; only the bare standalone use belongs in this dictionary. The spelling — American editing hyphenates it whenever it sits in front of a noun and leaves it open in the bare pronoun use, though both spellings turn up in both places.
entries.variants: such-and-such (hyphenated, the standard American written form); so-and-so for a person; thus and so and thus-and-such, both dated and now chiefly regional.
entries.see also: such, the like, this and that, whatnot, such-and-such (a) (determiner)

entries.meaning: Closes a list by standing in for the rest of its kind — "and other things like these."
examples: Bring rope, tape, zip ties, and the like.
The store carries feed, fencing, hand tools, and the like.
The policy covers floods, hurricanes, or the like.
He collects stamps, coins, and suchlike. (dated)
A crowd the like of which the town had never seen. (formal)
Did you ever see the like? (dated exclamation)
A different idiom: that club was never meant for the likes of us.
entries.pronunciation note: the is the ordinary weak /ðə/ before the consonant; like keeps its full diphthong and takes the stress, and the phrase has no reduced form
entries.русский: и тому подобное — закрывает перечисление, как русское «и т. п.»
entries.register: neutral to formal in and the like; the fixed exclamation Did you ever see the like? is dated, and suchlike is dated in American English
entries.type: pro-form standing for "other things of the same kind" — a category-closer
entries.person / number: invariant; notionally plural, but it takes a singular verb in the rare frames where it is a subject
entries.refers to: other things of the same kind as the ones just listed — the demonstrative version of et cetera, closing off a category instead of pointing inside it: bolts, washers, nuts, and the like. In the older the like of it means "an equal, a match": a crowd the like of which the town had never seen.
entries.agreement: in its ordinary use it is the object of and or or, so no agreement question arises. As a subject — dated, and chiefly in the negative — it is singular: The like has not been seen since.
entries.pattern: [list], and the like · [list], or the like · the like of which [clause] (formal, literary) · the likes of [noun phrase] (a different idiom — the likes of us, the likes of Amazon) · and suchlike (variant) · Did you ever see the like? (dated exclamation, still current in Irish and rural Southern American speech)
entries.contrast: Against and such — the same job, one register down: pens, paper, tape, and such is casual, and the like and and so on are neutral, and etc. is what the same sentence wears in a document. Against the likes of — the s changes the meaning completely: the likes of us means "people of our sort" and usually carries class feeling (not for the likes of us), where and the like only closes a list. Against such and such — a category to extend against a single blank to fill. The writing caution — a list closed with and the like is a list the writer has not finished defining, and in technical, legal, and contractual prose it is struck out for exactly that reason: the class stays open and nobody can say what is in it.
entries.variants: suchlike, one word (pens, paper, and suchlike) — dated in American English, still ordinary in British and Irish speech and heard in rural Southern American speech; it is also a determiner (suchlike nonsense), catalogued in the determiner dictionary. Regional American speech also has and the like of that.
entries.see also: such, such and such, so, the same, this and that, suchlike (determiner)

entries.meaning: Points back at something already named and marks the new instance as identical to it rather than merely similar.
examples: She ordered the salmon, and I'll have the same.
The same is true of every office we surveyed.
He left at five and expected everyone else to do the same.
The same goes for anyone who shows up after the doors close.
My rent is the same as it was three years ago.
Happy holidays! — Same to you. (informal)
We have received your order and will ship same on Monday. (commercial, dated)
entries.pronunciation note: the is the ordinary weak /ðə/ before a consonant sound; same carries the stress
entries.русский: то же самое — тождество с уже названным: I'll have the same «мне то же самое»
entries.register: neutral (I'll have the same); Same here is informal; bare same without the is commercial and legal, and dated
entries.type: demonstrative pro-form of identity
entries.person / number: invariant; the referent may be singular or plural
entries.refers to: a thing, an action, or a state of affairs already named, marked as identical to it rather than merely like it: She ordered the salmon and I'll have the same. It also points back at whole propositions — The same is true of the second quarter — and at actions, after do: He left at five and expected everyone else to do the same.
entries.agreement: it takes the number of what it stands for, and with an abstract or clause-sized referent it is singular: The same is true of the other branches. The same goes for you. With a plural referent a plural verb is grammatical but stiff, and American English prefers the same ones: The same ones are still on backorder rather than ?The same are still on backorder.
entries.pattern: [verb] the same (I'll have the same, Do the same) · the same as [noun phrase or clause] · The same goes for [noun phrase] · The same is true of [noun phrase] · Same here / Same to you (bare, informal reply) · remit / ship same (commercialese)
entries.contrast: Identity against resemblance — the same means one thing met twice; similar means two things that are alike. The comparison word is as, never like and never than: ✓ the same as last year, ✗ the same like last year, ✗ the same than last year. Bare same without the belongs to two registers only — casual replies (Same here, Same to you) and old commercial and legal writing (Enclosed is our invoice; kindly remit same), where every modern American style guide tells you to write it. Against the determiner same: the determiner needs a noun (the same problem); the pronoun stands alone.
entries.see also: such, so, one and the same, ditto, the like, that of, same (determiner)

entries.meaning: Points at an amount — or, in the frame this much is clear, at the one piece of a matter the speaker is prepared to vouch for, leaving the rest of it open.
examples: This much is clear: nobody read the contract before signing it.
I'll say this much for him — he showed up every single day.
We need a gallon of primer and I don't have that much.
That much I do know, whatever else is in dispute. (fronted, emphatic)
Don't worry about it that much; the deadline moved to the fifteenth.
This much I can tell you: the check was cashed on the fourth.
Countable referents take that many: ✗ that much were left over → that many were left over.
A different idiom altogether: so much for the quiet weekend I had planned.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form — much takes the stress and the demonstrative keeps its full vowel; in that much the /t/ is normally unreleased or a glottal stop before the /m/, [ˌðæʔˈmʌtʃ], so the two words sound welded together
entries.русский: столько — о количестве; и в обороте this much is clear «одно ясно» — об одной мысли
entries.register: neutral — ordinary in speech and in writing alike
entries.type: demonstrative + the degree quantifier much — a noun phrase standing for an amount, or for one measured piece of what is known
entries.person / number: third person singular, always; much is a mass quantifier and the phrase has no plural, the countable counterpart being this many / that many
entries.refers to: two things that look alike and are not. (1) A quantity just named, shown, or gestured at: We need a gallon. — I don't have that much. (2) A measured piece of what is known, in the frame this much is clear / I'll say this much, where the pronoun points forward at the one fact the speaker is willing to vouch for and quietly concedes that the rest is unsettled. Sense 2 is the one worth learning: it points at a proposition rather than at a substance, and it is a hedge as much as a pointer.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — This much is certain. That much was obvious to everybody. Never ✗ this much are, even when the fact it stands for involves several things at once. With a countable referent the phrase changes rather than the verb: That many were left over, not ✗ that much were left over.
entries.pattern: this much is clear / certain / true · I'll say this much (+ for [noun phrase]) · I know this much · [verb] that much (I don't have that much, we didn't drink that much) · not that much · that much I do know / this much I can tell you (fronted and contrastive) · so much for [noun phrase] (a separate idiom — see Contrast) · not this construction — this much money, that much trouble, determiner phrases sitting on a noun
entries.contrast: Sense 1 against sense 2 — the quantity use is literal and points at a heap or a volume (I don't have that much), while the pro-clause use points at a single fact (This much is clear), and only the second takes the frames I'll say this much and this much I know. Against as much — the closest relative in this file, and the line between them is worth keeping: as much stands for the whole proposition just stated and is a subject only in the one formal fronted frame As much was clear from the start, while this much stands for a portion of what is known and is a subject freely (This much is clear). Against so much — a different phrase doing three other jobs, none of them this one: so much for that dismisses something as finished, so much the better is a set comparative, and not so much opens a comparison. None of the three can be swapped in — ✗ So much is clear — which is why so much has no entry of its own here. Against this many / that many — mass against countable, and the line is hard: that much flour, that many eggs. Against the determiner — this much rain, that much trouble lean on a noun and belong with the determiners (much); only the standalone phrase is a pronoun.
entries.variants: that much I do know and this much I can tell you, the fronted emphatic order, idiomatic and common in speech; this little / that little at the opposite end (I didn't expect that little), which is rarer and always contrastive.
entries.see also: as much, so, not, the same, this, that, much, much (determiner)

entries.meaning: Tacks a further, often surprising, detail onto what was just said — "and what is more."
examples: He fixed it himself, and in ten minutes at that.
She found a buyer, and a cash buyer at that.
It's a long drive, and an ugly one at that.
He apologized once, and grudgingly at that.
We agreed to disagree and left it at that.
I'd rather not argue about it — let's leave it at that.
entries.pronunciation note: at reduces to /ət/ and its /t/ goes unreleased against the following /ð/ — [əˈðæt]
entries.русский: да ещё и, притом — в конце фразы; leave it at that «на том и остановиться»
entries.register: neutral to informal; chiefly spoken and in conversational writing
entries.type: fixed phrase — preposition plus demonstrative pronoun, working as a sentence-final connective
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: the thing or the fact just stated. Two idioms share the shape: sentence-final at that, meaning "and what's more," and leave it at that, meaning "stop there."
entries.agreement: none of its own — it modifies a clause and governs no verb.
entries.pattern: [clause], and [phrase] at that · [clause] — and a [adjective] one at that · leave it at that · let it go at that
entries.contrast: Sentence-final at that is not at that point or at that time, where that is a determiner sitting on a following noun. It always adds something: the phrase in front of it must be a further detail (and a cheap one at that), never a repetition of what was already said. Against besides and moreover, which do the same work in writing, at that is spoken, tail-end, and faintly wry. And leave it at that is a separate idiom that happens to share the words — it closes a subject rather than adding to one, and there it is closest to that's that.
entries.see also: that, that's that, with that, that said

entries.meaning: Introduces a restatement that narrows, corrects, or specifies what was just said.
examples: We'll meet on the first — that is, a week from Thursday.
He's her stepson, that is, her husband's boy from his first marriage.
The rule covers full-time employees, that is to say, anyone scheduled for thirty hours or more.
She'll be there Tuesday. If the flight lands, that is.
I'd like the small one — that is, if you can spare it.
The deadline is firm, that is, unless the client asks for an extension.
entries.pronunciation note: the /t/ flaps between the vowels — [ˌðæɾˈɪz]; the phrase is never contracted to ✗ that's in this use
entries.русский: то есть — связка, вводящая более точную формулировку сказанного
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in edited prose
entries.type: fixed phrase — demonstrative pronoun plus be, working as a discourse connective
entries.person / number: frozen in the third person singular; is never varies
entries.refers to: the word, phrase, or clause immediately before it, which the material after it then restates more precisely.
entries.agreement: always singular is — the phrase is frozen, and ✗ those are is not a plural version of it.
entries.pattern: [statement], that is, [restatement] · [statement] — that is — [restatement] · that is to say · sentence-final that is (He's coming Tuesday. If the flight's on time, that is.)
entries.contrast: that is is the English of Latin i.e. — "in other words, precisely" — while for example is e.g., "here is one instance among several." Interchanging the two is the commonest abbreviation error in American writing. Punctuation: American style puts commas on both sides (, that is,), and i.e. likewise takes a comma after it (i.e., the second draft). Against the neighbors built on the same pronoun: that said concedes and then pushes back, that's that closes a matter, and that's it either confirms a guess (Yes, that's it) or announces that something has run out.
entries.see also: that, that said, that's that, that's it

entries.meaning: Concedes the point just made and then turns against it — "even so."
examples: The car has 140,000 miles on it. That said, it's never once broken down.
I don't love the color. That said, it's a great price.
Attendance is down. That said, revenue is up nine percent.
He's inexperienced. That said, nobody prepares harder.
The evidence is thin. That said, the jury believed her.
We can't fund all of it — that said, we can cover the first phase.
entries.pronunciation note: no reduction; both words keep full vowels and the phrase takes its own intonation contour, set off by a comma
entries.русский: тем не менее, при этом — вводный оборот, отсылающий ко всей предыдущей уступке
entries.register: neutral; thoroughly established in business, academic, and journalistic prose
entries.type: fixed phrase — a nominative absolute in which the demonstrative pronoun is the participle's own subject, working as a connective
entries.person / number: invariant and frozen
entries.refers to: everything the writer has just conceded — the whole preceding sentence or paragraph, not a noun in it.
entries.agreement: none — the participle is non-finite, and the phrase governs no verb. The longer variants are that being said and having said that.
entries.pattern: [concession]. That said, [contrasting point] · [concession] — that said, [contrasting point] · That being said, … · Having said that, …
entries.contrast: Against however and nevertheless: that said first grants the previous point and then turns against it, so it needs a real concession in front of it — The design is expensive. That said, it will outlast three cheap ones. Its variants are simply longer, and editors cut that being said back to that said. One objection worth answering: that said is sometimes called a dangling modifier, but it is not — the pronoun that is the participle's own subject, which is what makes it an absolute construction. The form that really can dangle is having said that, which attaches itself to the subject of the main clause. Against at that and with that, which sit on the same pronoun: one adds a detail, one moves the story forward, and that said argues.
entries.see also: that, with that, that is, at that

entries.meaning: Confirms that something is exactly the thing meant — or announces that a supply, a process, or the speaker's patience has run out.
examples: Is the blue folder the one you wanted? — That's it.
Turn left after the church — no, wait, that's it, the brick one.
That's it for the questions; we're out of time.
We sold the last two this morning, so that was it.
That's it — I'm not driving back out there again. (exasperation)
Is that it, or is there another box still in the truck?
Sign at the bottom, and that's it — you're done.
entries.pronunciation note: the /s/ links straight onto the vowel of it — [ˌðæˈtsɪt] — and a final /t/ before a pause is usually unreleased or glottal, [ˈɪʔ]; the stress falls on it when the phrase confirms or protests, and on that's when it reports that something has ended
entries.русский: вот именно; всё, кончилось; ну всё, с меня хватит — разг., три разных употребления
entries.case: none — the demonstrative has no case forms, and it is the same shape in every slot
entries.register: informal to neutral; spoken far more often than written
entries.type: fixed clause — demonstrative pronoun as subject, the personal pronoun it as complement
entries.person / number: third person singular, frozen; the only other form is the narrative past that was it
entries.refers to: the thing, the guess, or the supply just mentioned or just pointed at. Three idioms share the shape: confirming that the hearer has hit on the right thing (Yes, that's it), reporting that a supply or a process has ended (That's it, we're out of forms), and, heavily stressed and usually with an exclamation point, announcing that the speaker's patience has run out (That's it — I'm leaving).
entries.agreement: singular is or was only — that's it, that was it. The idiom has no plural and no other tense; ✗ those are it is not a plural version of it.
entries.pattern: That's it (confirming) · That's it (supply or process ended) · That's it! (exasperation) · that's it for [noun phrase] · That was it (narrative past) · Is that it? (question)
entries.contrast: Three neighbors built on the same pronoun divide the work between them. that's that declares a matter closed against further argument; that's it confirms, or reports that something has run out; that's all is the mildest of the three, reporting only that nothing remains. There is a grammatical difference under the surface as well: in that's that both words are the demonstrative, while here the demonstrative is the subject and it is an ordinary personal pronoun — which is why this phrase turns into a question (Is that it?) and that's that does not (✗ Is that that?). And the exasperated That's it! is not the confirming one said louder: the intonation, not the words, carries that difference.
entries.see also: that's that, that is, that, at that, with that

entries.meaning: Declares a matter finished and not open to further discussion.
examples: The decision is final, and that's that.
She said no twice, so that was that.
If the bank won't lend, that's that — we don't buy the building.
He hung up, and that was that for the partnership.
We're not going. That's that.
One more late payment and that's that.
entries.pronunciation note: no reduction; the second that takes the stress, which is what makes the phrase sound final
entries.русский: вот и всё, и точка — вопрос закрыт, разг.
entries.case: none — English gives the demonstrative no case, which is why the same word fills both slots
entries.register: informal to neutral; spoken
entries.type: fixed clause — the demonstrative pronoun as both subject and complement
entries.person / number: third person singular, frozen
entries.refers to: the matter just settled: the first that points back at it, and the second closes it off.
entries.agreement: singular is or was only — that's that, that was that. There is no plural (✗ those are those) and no other tense in the idiom.
entries.pattern: and that's that · that was that (narrative past) · if [clause], then that's that · [statement]. That's that.
entries.contrast: That's that declares a matter closed and not open to discussion. That's it does two other jobs — confirming that a guess is right (Yes, that's it) and announcing that a supply or a process has ended (That's it, we're out of forms). That's all is weaker still: it merely reports that nothing remains. And leave it at that asks for the same closure politely, where that's that imposes it.
entries.see also: that, at that, that is, that's it, with that

entries.meaning: Various unspecified things — the polite way of not saying what.
examples: We talked about this and that for the better part of an hour.
I spent the weekend doing this and that around the house.
She's been busy with this and that since she retired.
It's a bit of this and that — nothing you'd call a system.
He kept asking about this, that, and the other thing.
What did you buy? — Oh, this and that.
entries.pronunciation note: and reduces to /ən/ or to a syllabic /n/ — [ˌðɪsn̩ˈðæt]
entries.русский: то да сё — разг., о разных мелочах, которые говорящий не хочет перечислять
entries.register: informal
entries.type: fixed coordinate phrase of two demonstrative pronouns
entries.person / number: invariant; notionally plural but grammatically frozen
entries.refers to: unspecified miscellaneous things, tasks, or topics — deliberately vague, because the speaker is declining to itemize.
entries.agreement: it almost always appears as the object of a verb or a preposition rather than as a subject, so the question rarely arises; where a subject is needed, speakers reach for a few things or odds and ends instead.
entries.pattern: talk about this and that · do this and that · a bit of this and that · this, that, and the other (thing) (the three-part extension)
entries.contrast: This is the demonstrative version of et cetera, vague on purpose. This and that covers topics and small tasks; odds and ends covers physical objects; this, that, and the other thing stretches the same joke to three. The word order is fixed — ✗ that and this — and so is the and: this or that is not a variant of the idiom but a different phrase altogether, one that offers a genuine choice between two.
entries.see also: this, that, such

entries.term: this is he / this is she
entries.meaning: The American telephone answer meaning "I am the person you are asking for."
examples: May I speak with Diane Palmer? — This is she.
Is Mr. Okafor available? — This is he.
Am I speaking to the account holder? — You are; this is he.
Is this Dr. Ruiz? — This is her, but I'm with a patient. (ordinary speech)
Can I talk to whoever handles billing? — This is she. What can I do for you?
Hi, is this Karen? — This is Karen, yes.
entries.pronunciation note: in the everyday version the personal pronoun takes its weak form — this is him [ˈðɪsɪzɪm], this is her [ˈðɪsɪzɚ] — while the formal he and she stay strong, which is part of why they sound formal
entries.русский: это я, я у телефона — офиц. ответ на просьбу позвать к телефону; разг. this is him / her
entries.case: subject case in the formal version (he, she); object case in the ordinary spoken one (him, her)
entries.register: formal and business-standard (this is he / this is she); neutral (this is him / this is her, speaking)
entries.type: fixed telephone formula — demonstrative pronoun + be + personal pronoun as subject complement
entries.person / number: third person singular in form, first person in meaning — the speaker refers to himself or herself in the third person, a quirk unique to this formula
entries.refers to: the speaker, identified as the person the caller asked for.
entries.agreement: singular is. The pronoun that follows agrees with the speaker's own gender, which is the only place gender enters the demonstrative system.
entries.pattern: May I speak to Ms. Ruiz? — This is she. · Is Mr. Okafor available? — This is he. · Speaking. · This is [name] (self-identification) · Is this Karen? — This is Karen.
entries.contrast: The traditional rule says that the complement of be takes the subject case, which gives This is he and This is she — the same rule behind It is I. American speech went the other way long ago: It's me is standard, and This is him / This is her is what most Americans actually say. What keeps This is he/she alive is register rather than the rule. It is the receptionist's and the customer-service answer, and in that one setting it sounds crisp rather than stiff, where It is I would sound absurd anywhere at all. Both are safe on the phone; the dodge that avoids the question entirely is Speaking or This is Karen. Note also that this is close to the only everyday context in which Americans use a subject-case pronoun after be without irony — It was he who signed still turns up in formal writing, but nowhere in speech — and that British speakers, who normally answer Speaking, find This is she distinctly American.
entries.see also: this, that, that's that, the grammar of pronouns: It is I vs It's me

entries.meaning: Marks the immediate next action after something just said or done — "and on that note."
examples: With that, she picked up her coat and left.
He signed the form, and with that the sale was final.
With that, the meeting broke up.
She thanked the jury, and with that the trial was over.
He set the box on the counter and, with that, walked out.
With that, the lights went down and the show began.
entries.pronunciation note: the two /ð/ sounds merge into a single long one — [wɪˈðæt]; American with is voiced /wɪð/ before another voiced sound
entries.русский: с этими словами; на этом — сказав или сделав только что описанное
entries.register: neutral to literary; a device of narrative and reportage
entries.type: fixed phrase — preposition plus demonstrative pronoun, working as a narrative connective
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: the words or the action just reported. With that means "having said that" or "having done that."
entries.agreement: none of its own; it modifies the clause that follows.
entries.pattern: With that, [subject] [verb] · And with that, … · [clause], and with that [clause] · with that said (a blend of with that and that said — common in speech, redundant in writing)
entries.contrast: Three connectives in this file are built on the same pronoun and none of them is interchangeable. With that is temporal and dramatic: the next thing happens immediately, and because of what just happened. that said is concessive: it grants a point and then argues against it. at that adds a further detail to what was just said. The blend with that being said is wordy on both ends and gets cut to that said.
entries.see also: that, that said, at that, that's that

entries.meaning: That, with the distance emphasized. Nonstandard.
examples: That there is my truck. (nonstandard)
Hand me that there, would you? (nonstandard)
That there's the one that's been leaking. (nonstandard)
I'll take that there and two of the little ones. (nonstandard)
That there ain't going to hold. (nonstandard)
Standard: That one is my truck.
entries.pronunciation note: in fast speech the whole phrase collapses to [ˈðæɾɚ], written that'ere in dialect fiction
entries.русский: вон тот — прост., диал. (юж. и сельский амер.); усиленное указание вдаль
entries.register: nonstandard — rural and Southern American speech, and the standard shorthand for it in fiction and film
entries.type: nonstandard emphatic demonstrative pronoun
entries.person / number: third person singular
entries.refers to: one thing at a distance, with the pointing reinforced. Standard English puts the there after the noun phrase (that one there); this dialect pulls it inside.
entries.agreement: singular verb — That there is my truck.
entries.pattern: that there + [singular verb] · [verb] that there · that there's (contracted) · the determiner use that there truck, covered in the determiner dictionary
entries.contrast: Standard equivalents are that, that one, that one there, and that one over there. The plural is them there or those there. It is not an intensifier a learner can borrow: writing it outside dialogue marks the writer, not the speaker. Compare the parallel near forms this here and these here.
entries.see also: this here, these here, those there, them there, them, that

entries.meaning: Those. Nonstandard outside a handful of fixed idioms.
examples: Them are the ones I want. (nonstandard)
Them's the breaks. (fixed idiom, jocular even in standard speech)
Them's fightin' words. (fixed idiom)
I'll take them in the back there. (nonstandard)
Them was good times. (nonstandard, with the dialect singular verb)
Them ain't none of mine. (nonstandard; negative concord — the double negative — riding along with it)
Standard: Those are the ones I want.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ðəm/, and after a consonant frequently just /əm/ — give me 'em; the reduction is ordinary and standard, and it is the demonstrative use that is not
entries.русский: те, вон те — прост., диал. вместо those (не личное местоимение «их»): Them are the ones
entries.case: historically the object case, but in this use it appears as a subject as well (Them are the ones)
entries.register: nonstandard — widespread in rural, Southern, and working-class American speech, and frozen inside a few idioms everyone knows
entries.type: nonstandard demonstrative pronoun — the object pronoun them standing in for those
entries.person / number: third person plural
entries.refers to: plural things or people at a distance — the dialect equivalent of those.
entries.agreement: plural verb in most dialects — Them are the ones I want — though the same varieties often use a singular (Them was good times), which is a separate dialect feature riding along with it.
entries.pattern: them + plural verb (Them are the ones) · [verb] them (indistinguishable from the ordinary personal pronoun) · them there · the determiner use them apples, covered in the determiner dictionary · frozen: Them's the breaks, Them's fightin' words
entries.contrast: In standard English them is only the object form of they (I saw them) and can never be a subject or a demonstrative: ✗ Them are mine → Those are mine; ✗ I'll take them apples → those apples. The tell is position — a them in subject position, or a them sitting directly in front of a noun, is dialect. Do not confuse the use with the pronunciation: the reduced /əm/ of I saw 'em is ordinary standard American speech and carries no dialect marking at all. The fixed idioms Them's the breaks and Them's fightin' words are quoted by standard speakers as jokes, complete with the dialect verb.
entries.see also: those, them there, those there, that there, them (determiner)

entries.meaning: Those, with the distance emphasized twice over. Nonstandard.
examples: Them there are the ones we cut last fall. (nonstandard)
Load up them there and let's get going. (nonstandard)
Them there's the ones I told you about. (nonstandard, contracted)
I wouldn't give a nickel for them there. (nonstandard)
Are them there for sale? (nonstandard)
Them there ain't ripe yet. (nonstandard)
Standard: Those are the ones we cut last fall.
entries.pronunciation note: no reduction; the two words run together as one stressed unit, and the eye-dialect spelling of it is them thar
entries.русский: вон те — прост., диал.; сильно маркированная форма, мн. число к that there
entries.case: none as a demonstrative; the them is historically the object form of they, and in this use it stands as a subject as well (Them there are the ones)
entries.register: nonstandard — rural and Southern American speech, heavily marked, and the stock phrase of dialect comedy
entries.type: nonstandard emphatic demonstrative pronoun (plural, far) — nonstandard them with the reinforcing there pulled in front of it
entries.person / number: third person plural
entries.refers to: more than one thing at a distance, with the pointing doubly reinforced. It is the plural partner of that there, and within the dialects that have these forms it is commoner than those there.
entries.agreement: plural verb — Them there are the ones I meant. The same varieties often use a singular instead (Them there was the good ones), which is a separate dialect feature riding along and not a property of the phrase.
entries.pattern: them there + plural verb · [verb] them there · [preposition] them there · them there's (contracted) · them thar (eye-dialect spelling; the famous There's gold in them thar hills is the determiner use) · the determiner use them there hills, covered in the determiner dictionary
entries.contrast: It doubles two nonstandard features at once — them standing in for those, and there wedged in front of the pronoun instead of trailing after it. Standard equivalents are those, those over there, and the ones over there: standard English reinforces the pointing too, but always after the phrase (those right there), never inside it. The near counterpart is these here, the singular is that there, and the them-less variant is those there. In print it signals dialect; from a standard speaker it is nearly always deliberate humor.
entries.see also: them, that there, those there, these here, those, them there (determiner)

entries.meaning: These, with the nearness emphasized. Nonstandard.
examples: These here are the good ones. (nonstandard)
These here ain't ripe yet. (nonstandard)
I'll take these here and leave the rest. (nonstandard)
These here were my grandfather's. (nonstandard)
What about these here? (nonstandard)
Standard: These are the good ones. / These right here are the good ones.
entries.pronunciation note: no reduction; the /h/ is often dropped in fast speech — [ˌðizˈɪr]
entries.русский: вот эти — прост., диал.; усиленное указание на близкое
entries.register: nonstandard — rural and Southern American speech; dialect writing
entries.type: nonstandard emphatic demonstrative pronoun (plural, near)
entries.person / number: third person plural
entries.refers to: more than one thing close to the speaker, with the nearness underlined.
entries.agreement: plural verb — These here are the good ones.
entries.pattern: these here + plural verb · [verb] these here · the determiner use these here boots, covered in the determiner dictionary
entries.contrast: Standard equivalents: these, these ones (speech only), the ones here. The distal counterpart is those there, and the singular is this here. Standard English can emphasize nearness too, but it puts the adverb after the phrase — these right here — rather than inside it.
entries.see also: this here, that there, those there, these

entries.meaning: This, with the nearness emphasized. Nonstandard.
examples: This here is my brother Delbert. (nonstandard)
This here's the one that needs fixing. (nonstandard)
Take this here on out to the barn. (nonstandard)
This here don't look right to me. (nonstandard)
How much for this here? (nonstandard)
Standard: This is my brother Delbert.
entries.pronunciation note: no reduction; the /h/ is often dropped — [ˌðɪsˈɪr]
entries.русский: вот этот — прост., диал.; усиленное указание на близкое, мн. число these here
entries.register: nonstandard — rural and Southern American speech; dialect writing
entries.type: nonstandard emphatic demonstrative pronoun (singular, near)
entries.person / number: third person singular
entries.refers to: one thing close to the speaker, with the nearness underlined. It can introduce a person, exactly as standard this does: This here is my brother.
entries.agreement: singular verb — This here is my brother.
entries.pattern: this here + singular verb · [verb] this here · this here's (contracted) · the determiner use this here dog, covered in the determiner dictionary
entries.contrast: Standard equivalents: this, this one, this one right here. The distal counterpart is that there and the plural is these here. As with all four, standard English adds the emphasis after the pronoun (this one right here), never inside it.
entries.see also: these here, that there, those there, this

entries.meaning: Those, with the distance emphasized. Nonstandard.
examples: Those there are the ones we cut last fall. (nonstandard)
Bring me those there off the top shelf. (nonstandard)
Those there won't fit through the door. (nonstandard)
I never did trust those there. (nonstandard)
Are those there for sale? (nonstandard)
Standard: Those are the ones we cut last fall.
entries.pronunciation note: no reduction; in the dialects that use it, them there is the more frequent form
entries.русский: вон те — прост., диал.; усиленное указание вдаль
entries.register: nonstandard — rural and Southern American speech; dialect writing
entries.type: nonstandard emphatic demonstrative pronoun (plural, far)
entries.person / number: third person plural
entries.refers to: more than one thing at a distance, with the pointing reinforced.
entries.agreement: plural verb — Those there are the ones we cut last fall.
entries.pattern: those there + plural verb · [verb] those there · them there (the commoner dialect form) · the determiner use those there boards, covered in the determiner dictionary
entries.contrast: Standard equivalents: those, those ones (speech only), the ones over there. Within the dialect itself, them there is more usual than those there — the them form and the there reinforcement travel together. The near counterpart is these here.
entries.see also: that there, these here, them there, them, those

entries.meaning: That one over there — archaic, and pointing at what is far from everyone present.
examples: Yon is the house where he was born. (archaic)
Whose land is yon, beyond the creek? (archaic, regional)
He looked from this to yon and said nothing. (literary)
Yon was the ridge we crossed at dawn. (archaic)
The papers were scattered hither and yon. (fixed phrase, current)
Modern: That is the house where he was born.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; one syllable, always stressed
entries.русский: вон тот — устар., диал.; третья степень дальности: this — that — yon
entries.register: archaic and literary; regional in Appalachian and Ozark speech, and alive in Scots and Northern English
entries.type: archaic demonstrative pronoun of the third, far degree
entries.person / number: invariant — no singular/plural distinction at all, which is part of what makes it sound old
entries.refers to: something visible but far from speaker and hearer alike — the third term of a system English has otherwise lost (this by me, that by you, yon over there), the one Spanish still keeps as este / ese / aquel.
entries.agreement: the verb follows the referent, since the form itself never changes: Yon is the house / Yon are the hills we crossed. In practice the pronoun use is rare even in the dialects that keep the word; the determiner (yon ridge) and the adverb yonder carry nearly all of it.
entries.pattern: yon as subject (Yon is the house) · [preposition] yon · hither and yon (fixed adverbial, "here and there" — the one fully current use) · the determiner use yon ridge, covered in the determiner dictionary
entries.contrast: Modern standard English has collapsed the old three-way system into two, so that now covers everything yon once did. Of the three surviving forms, only yonder is still said by Americans, and mostly as an adverb (over yonder); yon survives in verse, in hymns, and in the fixed hither and yon; yond is a Shakespeare quotation and nothing more. None of the three belongs in ordinary writing.
entries.see also: yonder, that, those, yon (determiner), yond (determiner)

entries.meaning: That thing over there, in sight — archaic as a pronoun, current as a regional adverb of place.
examples: Yonder is the schoolhouse my grandmother taught in. (archaic, regional)
Yonder are the hills we crossed. (archaic)
Yonder was the mill, before the fire took it. (archaic)
The cabin is just over yonder. (adverb — the ordinary use)
He's out yonder mending fence. (regional adverb)
They lit out for the wild blue yonder. (fixed noun phrase)
Modern standard: That is the schoolhouse. / It's over there.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; stressed on the first syllable, with the r-colored /ɚ/ of General American
entries.русский: вон тот, вон там — устар. как местоимение; как наречие живо в юж. амер. говоре
entries.register: archaic as a pronoun; regional but thoroughly alive as an adverb — Southern, Appalachian, Ozark, and rural Midwestern
entries.type: archaic demonstrative pronoun; far more commonly an adverb of place, which is the living use
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: something at middle-to-far distance and in view. As a pronoun (Yonder is the schoolhouse) it is archaic and biblical-sounding; as an adverb (He's out yonder) it is ordinary regional American speech.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the noun phrase that follows, which is the real subject: Yonder is the schoolhouse, Yonder are the hills. That is itself the clue that most apparent pronoun uses are really a fronted adverb with the subject behind the verb.
entries.pattern: Yonder is / are + [noun phrase] · over yonder, out yonder, up yonder, down yonder (adverb — the living use) · the wild blue yonder (fixed noun phrase) · the determiner use yonder field, covered in the determiner dictionary
entries.contrast: Against that: that means simply "not here," while yonder adds "and you can see it from where we stand" — a distance judged by eye. Against yon and yond: three forms of one word, of which yonder is the only one an American still says. And the part-of-speech caution matters most — nearly every modern yonder is an adverb (He's out yonder) or a determiner (yonder field), not a pronoun, so a learner needs it for listening rather than for writing.
